_podcast.theme_scoring_prompt:
Rate how well this article fits the theme 'Indigenous Lands & Innovation' — Indigenous nations using technology, governance, and stewardship on their own terms.

OUT OF SCOPE — score 0-9: geopolitical and war news with no Indigenous rights angle; general wildfire and wildlife-service updates not led by or directly affecting Indigenous communities or guardians; provincial forestry and environmental policy with no explicit First Nations involvement; consumer tech and gadget reviews; science with no Indigenous stewardship or sovereignty context; crime and judicial news unrelated to Indigenous rights.

CALIBRATION — apply this ladder to everything else. Indigenous-led journalism on governance, rights, and self-determination is a strong fit on its own: a technology hook raises a score but is NOT required to reach the top band.
- 80-100: Excellent Indigenous-led reporting. Cariboo stories bridging governance or culture AND technology land here (Tŝilhqot'in/Secwépemc/Dakelh language revitalization tech, guardian programs using sensors and drones, GIS land mapping, Indigenous-led connectivity, digital heritage projects) — and so does outstanding national coverage of sovereignty, treaty, and land rights.
- 55-79: Solid pan-Canadian Indigenous governance, sovereignty, land rights, treaty, or reconciliation journalism — APTN, Eagle Feather News, or IndigiNews-style coverage of First Nations governance, MMIWG, land claims, self-determination, and Indigenous-led services. Most Indigenous governance journalism belongs HERE, not below.
- 30-54: Indigenous cultural, community, or human-interest stories (awards, events, ceremonies) with limited governance substance, or BC land-stewardship and environmental stories with meaningful First Nations involvement.
- 10-29: General BC land, environmental, or forestry stories that mention Indigenous communities only in passing.

ANCHORS: 'Tŝilhqot'in Nation launches drone-based caribou monitoring on title lands' → 98. 'First Nations leaders reject BC's revised land-title framework' → 75. 'Secwépemc language app reaches 1,000 learners' → 88. 'BC Wildfire Service updates evacuation alerts for the Interior' → 8.

Score 0-100 where 100 is a perfect thematic match and 0 is completely unrelated.

items.title: [Macworld] Should you buy a Mac mini now? M6 vs M5 Pro buying advice
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Macworld

The Mac mini received a major update in August 2026, so for most people this is a good time to buy. Apple announced the new M6 and M5 Pro Mac mini on August 25, 2026, with sales beginning September 22. With the next significant update unlikely for some time, there is little reason to wait for newer hardware if you need a compact desktop Mac now.

For most buyers, we recommend the M6 Mac mini. Starting at $899/£899, it is considerably more expensive than the M4 generation, which launched at $599, but it offers improved performance for everyday work, office tasks, coding, photo and video editing, and general creative use. It is particularly appealing if you already own a monitor, keyboard and mouse, or if you’re replacing an older Intel Mac or early Apple silicon model.

The M5 Pro Mac mini is better suited to more demanding users. Its additional CPU and GPU performance, Thunderbolt 5 connectivity, higher memory bandwidth and support for up to 64GB of unified memory make it a stronger choice for professional creative work, development and larger local AI models. However, with prices starting at $1,699/£1,699 and rising quickly with upgrades, most people won’t need to spend that much.

This guide explains whether to buy a Mac mini now, which M6 or M5 Pro model suits different users, what to pay, alternatives, refurbished options, drawbacks, and where to buy.

Should you buy a Mac mini now?

There are reasons to wait. Discounts are likely to improve in the months after launch, particularly around Prime Day in October and Black Friday in November, and more refurbished or discounted M4 models may appear as buyers upgrade. If you’re happy with your current Mac, want to see independent benchmarks first or simply want the lowest possible price, there is no need to rush.

On the other hand, buyers who want a new Mac mini at launch may prefer to pre-order. A global memory shortage contributed to long delivery times and limited availability for the previous generation, and similar supply constraints could affect the new models. The higher cost of memory and other components has also contributed to the Mac mini’s substantial price increase.

Buy Mac mini now if:

  • You need a Mac mini now and want the latest model.
  • You’re replacing an Intel Mac or an older Apple silicon Mac.
  • You want a powerful compact desktop for everyday, office, development or creative work.
  • The $899/£899 M6 Mac mini provides all the performance you need.

Consider M5 Pro if:

  • You need more than 32GB of unified memory.
  • You run demanding professional creative or development workloads.
  • You want to run larger local AI or LLM workloads.
  • You need Thunderbolt 5 or substantially greater memory bandwidth.

Wait if:

  • You want to see independent benchmarks of the new models.
  • You’re hoping for discounts around Prime Day or Black Friday.
  • Your current Mac still meets your needs.
  • You don’t need a new Mac urgently and want to see whether prices fall.

Consider refurbished if:

  • You can find an M4 Mac mini at a significant discount.
  • You want the best value rather than the newest chip.
  • An Apple-refurbished M4 or M4 Pro configuration meets your memory and storage needs.
  • You’re comfortable waiting for refurbished M6 or M5 Pro stock to appear.

Apple Mac mini (M6, 2026)

Price When Reviewed: $899
Best Prices Today: $899 at Apple

Apple Mac mini (M5 Pro, 2026)

Price When Reviewed: $1,699
Best Prices Today: $1699 at Apple

Which Mac mini to buy: M6 or M5 Pro?

Simon Jary / Foundry

The Mac mini lineup has changed significantly in 2026, with Apple introducing the M6 and M5 Pro models in August. The choice between them comes down to your workload and budget, as they serve very different audiences despite sharing the same compact design.

Apple sells two Mac mini models, both announced on August 25 and shipping from September 22, 2026:

Mac mini (M6) — starts at $899 / £899

  • 12-core CPU, 12-core GPU
  • 16GB unified memory (up to 32GB)
  • Up to 2TB SSD
  • Thunderbolt 4 (three ports), two front USB-C ports, HDMI, 2.5Gb Ethernet
  • Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6
  • Supports up to three displays (two 6K + one 5K)

Mac mini (M5 Pro) — starts at $1,699 / £1,699

  • 15-core CPU, 16-core GPU (upgradeable to 18-core CPU, 20-core GPU for +$200)
  • 24GB unified memory (up to 64GB)
  • Up to 8TB SSD
  • Thunderbolt 5 (three ports), two front USB-C ports, HDMI, 2.5Gb Ethernet
  • Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6
  • Supports up to three 6K displays

Despite the “M5” name being a generation older than “M6,” the M5 Pro is the more powerful chip — it has more CPU and GPU cores, nearly double the memory bandwidth (307GB/s vs 170GB/s), and supports far more unified memory.

Choose the M6 Mac mini if:

  • You don’t need more than 32GB of unified memory (RAM).
  • You need a compact, powerful desktop for everyday use – web browsing, office work, photo editing, coding, and general productivity.
  • You’re a student or budget-conscious buyer looking for the best-value option for home offices, school or office use. Education pricing brings the starting price down to $799.
  • You already own a monitor, keyboard, and mouse.
  • You don’t need the extra performance or connectivity of the M5 Pro model.

Choose the M5 Pro Mac mini if:

  • You’re a developer, video editor, 3D artist, musician, or researcher who needs sustained performance for demanding workloads.
  • You want to run larger local AI models. The M5 Pro’s higher memory ceiling and much greater memory bandwidth make it better suited to heavier LLM workloads than the M6. If local AI is a priority, choose your memory carefully because it cannot be upgraded later.
  • You need Thunderbolt 5 for faster external storage, high-bandwidth peripherals or professional video workflows.
  • You regularly work with heavy 3D rendering, high-end video production, large codebases or scientific workloads.
  • You need more than 32GB of unified memory.

How much should you pay for Mac mini?

  • M6 Mac mini, starting at $899.
  • M5 Pro Mac mini, starting at $1,699.

Since the August 2026 update, the Mac mini is no longer the budget Mac it once was. The M6 model starts at $899, $300 more than the $599 starting price of the M4 generation.

For most people, the $899 M6 Mac mini is the model to buy. It offers more than enough performance for everyday work, browsing, media and general productivity, although the standard 16GB of unified memory and 256GB SSD may feel limiting if you plan to keep it for several years.

If you need more demanding performance for creative work, development or running local AI models, the M5 Pro Mac mini starts at $1,699. Configurations with more memory and storage can quickly push the price towards $3,000, so it only makes sense if you genuinely need that extra performance.

Be cautious about spending heavily on Apple’s storage upgrades. External SSDs and Mac mini hubs with NVMe storage can provide considerably more capacity for less money.

For most buyers, we recommend spending around $899 on the M6 Mac mini. Move up to the M5 Pro only if you need its extra processing power or significantly more memory.

Discounts are likely to appear at Amazon and other resellers over time, particularly around Prime Day in October and Black Friday in November. For now, the best bargain may be a discounted M4 Mac mini, although remaining stock is likely to be limited.

Find Apple on Amazon U.S.

Find Apple on Amazon U.K.

Students can save $100 through Apple’s Education Store, reducing the M6 Mac mini to $799 and the M5 Pro model to $1,599. Apple’s Refurbished Store is another way to save, although it may be some time before the new M6 and M5 Pro models appear there. Read: How to get an Apple student discount at Apple’s Education Store and Should you buy a refurbished Mac.

Reasons to buy a Mac mini

Foundry

Excellent value: The price has gone up, but the Mac mini remains one of the most versatile and cost-effective ways to enter the macOS ecosystem. Even at the new starting price of $899, the Mac mini still delivers excellent performance per dollar. That balance of price, power, and efficiency is one of the main reasons for the desktop’s growing popularity. It also offers access to professional-grade performance for significantly less cash than a similarly specced MacBook Pro.

Long software support window: The M6 and M5 Pro Mac mini will have a long usable lifespan and will receive many years of macOS updates and security support.

Compact desktop footprint: The Mac mini’s ultra-compact 5-inch square design makes it one of the most space-efficient desktop computers available. It fits easily under monitors, in small offices, or in minimalist workstation setups. Its compact form factor also makes it particularly attractive for server racks, home labs, and multi-machine deployments. 

Retail discounts and refurbished deals: Despite already offering strong value at full price, the Mac mini is occasionally discounted by third-party retailers. If you can find a Mac mini deal – even on a M4 model with a higher-memory configuration – we recommend taking advantage of it. The Apple Refurbished Store can offer even better value, assuming stock is available. In the past, we have seen the M4 Mac mini discounted by around $100/£100, while M4 Pro models have dropped by approximately $200/£210. If deals like these reappear, they are likely worth considering.

Reasons not to buy Mac mini

The price has gone up significantly: The Mac mini was once the undisputed budget Mac, but that is much harder to say now. The entry-level model has risen sharply in price, making it less compelling for buyers primarily looking for the cheapest way into the Mac ecosystem. At $899, the latest Mac mini is still less expensive than a MacBook or iMac, but it no longer feels like the bargain it once was.

You need to buy your own peripherals: The Mac mini is a “BYODKM” – Bring Your Own Display, Keyboard and Mouse – computer. That’s central to its appeal if you already own those accessories, but it can add substantially to the cost if you don’t. Unlike an iMac or MacBook, the Mac mini doesn’t include a display, keyboard or mouse. Buying all three can easily add hundreds of dollars to the overall price. The latest models also lack USB-A ports, so you may need adapters or a hub if you still use older accessories.

It’s not portable: The Mac mini is a desktop computer, so it isn’t suitable if you need to work in different locations. You can’t easily take it to a lecture, meeting or coffee shop in the way you can a MacBook. For students, frequent travellers or anyone who regularly works away from a desk, a laptop is likely to be the better choice.

You can’t upgrade it later: You need to choose your memory and storage carefully when you buy because neither can be upgraded afterwards. Apple’s build-to-order memory and storage upgrades can also be expensive, particularly once you start moving beyond the base configuration. This can quickly push the Mac mini into MacBook Pro or Mac Studio territory. Storage is less of a concern because inexpensive external SSDs and Mac mini hubs with NVMe storage can add capacity later, but there is no equivalent workaround for unified memory.

Availability could be limited: New Mac launches can sometimes bring longer delivery times for popular configurations, particularly higher-memory or build-to-order models. The M6 and M5 Pro Mac mini may suffer significant shortages due to their popularity and the shortage of components and memory.

It’s not ideal for every AI workload: Apple is increasingly positioning its Macs for AI workloads, but as our colleagues at PCWorld explain, the Mac mini has some limitations if running large local models is your main priority. The standard M6 Mac mini tops out at 32GB of unified memory, which may be restrictive for particularly large local models. The M5 Pro model offers more memory, but higher-spec configurations become expensive quickly. There is also no support for Nvidia’s CUDA platform. Many professional AI and machine-learning tools are optimized around CUDA and Nvidia GPUs, so a Windows or Linux PC with a suitable Nvidia graphics card may be faster or better supported for some workloads. For general Apple Intelligence features and lighter local AI use, however, this shouldn’t be a concern.

What to avoid when buying a Mac mini

IDG

Intel: Avoid Intel-powered Mac mini models – when shopping for a refurbished Mac mini, prioritize models with Apple Silicon (M-series chips). 

Low RAM: We advise avoiding 8GB RAM models if possible, as newer generations now start with 16GB as the base standard. 

Check status: Additionally, ensure the device is not classified as “Vintage” or “Obsolete,” as Apple typically stops providing parts for repairs after seven to ten years. 

Is Mac mini right for you?

Is the Mac mini the best choice for you? There are a number of trade-offs to consider. 

Who is the Mac mini best for?

Mac mini vs Mac Studio: Which should you buy?

Thomas Bergbold

The choice between the Mac mini and the Mac Studio largely comes down to whether you prioritize value or maximum performance.

The Mac mini offers some of the best value in Apple’s desktop lineup. Even the standard M6 model delivers impressive performance for everyday computing, creative work, software development, and local AI tasks, while the M5 Pro configuration provides power for more demanding workloads.

The Mac Studio is designed for users who need workstation-class performance. Following the discontinuation of the Mac Pro, it is now effectively Apple’s most powerful desktop. Starting at $2,499/£2,499 for the M5 Max configuration, the Mac Studio also represents the most affordable way to get a Max-series Apple Silicon chip (which starts at $4,099/£4,099 if you buy a MacBook Pro). It is well suited to professional video production, large AI models, 3D rendering, and other heavily multi-threaded or GPU-intensive workflows.

For most users, the Mac mini is a better value purchase. However, if your workloads demand high performance, more memory and a more powerful GPU, the Mac Studio is the better choice. 

Mac mini vs MacBook Neo: Which is better value?

Thomas Armbrüster

Before the introduction of the MacBook Neo, the Mac mini was Apple’s least expensive Mac. That is no longer the case – particularly now Apple has raised the price of the entry-level Mac mini from $599/£599 to $899/£899.

The MacBook Neo is now Apple’s most affordable Mac, starting at $699/£699. It is designed as an entry-level Mac and is powered by the A18 Pro chip originally used for the iPhone 16 Pro and only offers 8GB memory. The focus is on portability, battery life, and affordability rather than performance.

The Mac mini, by contrast, remains Apple’s best-value desktop Mac for users who already own a monitor, keyboard, and mouse. Thanks to its M6 and M5 Pro chips, active cooling system, and greater performance, it is better suited to demanding workloads such as coding, creative applications, multitasking, and local AI development.

Where to buy a Mac mini

If you’re looking to buy a Mac mini, you can choose between Apple, third-party retailers and refurbished outlets.

Apple: You can buy a Mac mini directly from the Apple Store online or at an Apple retail store.

Apple Education Store: Apple also offers discounted education pricing for eligible students and educators via its Education Store. For example, the $899 M6 Mac mini costs $799 with education pricing.

Third-Party Resellers: It’s worth checking third-party retailers as well as Apple, as stores such as Amazon and B&H frequently discount Macs. Authorized resellers and major retailers often sell the Mac mini at less than Apple’s list price.

In the U.S., retailers include:

  • Amazon
  • Best Buy
  • B&H Photo Video
  • Costco
  • Adorama
  • DataVision

In the U.K., retailers include:

  • Amazon
  • Argos
  • Currys
  • John Lewis
  • AO
  • Ebuyer
  • Laptops Direct

The U.K. also has Apple Premium Resellers including KRCS, iStore, Select, Albion and Jigsaw.

Should you buy a refurbished Mac mini?

A refurbished Mac mini can be an excellent way to save money, particularly if you don’t need the latest model. Discounts can be significant, although the exact saving depends on the model, configuration and seller.

The best place to start is Apple’s Refurbished Store. Apple’s refurbished Macs are fully tested, cleaned and inspected, and come with a one-year limited warranty, 90 days of technical support and eligibility for AppleCare. They are also supplied with the appropriate accessories and repackaged in a new box.

Earlier in 2026, we saw refurbished M4 Mac mini models discounted by around $90/£90, with savings also available on the M4 Pro version. However, as of September 2026, refurbished Mac mini stock is very limited. M4 models are currently unavailable, and it may be some time before the new M6 and M5 Pro models start appearing in Apple’s refurbished store.

Availability is one of the main drawbacks of buying refurbished. Stock depends on returns and trade-ins, so you may not find the exact memory or storage configuration you want. More models may become available as owners upgrade to the latest Mac minis and older machines make their way to refurbishers.

You should also be careful when buying from third-party sellers. Refurbishment standards and warranties can vary, and marketplaces may contain much older Intel-based Mac minis. We generally wouldn’t recommend those models now unless the price is exceptionally low, as Apple silicon Mac minis offer much better performance and will receive software support for longer.

We’ve found Amazon particularly worth checking carefully. Refurbished stock can be dominated by Mac minis from 2020 or earlier, and we’ve even seen discontinued configurations listed for more than their original selling price. Always check the model year, specification and price of an equivalent new Mac before buying.

Buying refurbished is generally safer than buying second hand from a private seller. A reputable refurbished Mac should have been inspected and tested and will usually include a warranty and returns policy. A privately sold Mac may offer neither, and there is also a risk of Activation Lock if the previous owner hasn’t properly removed the Mac from their Apple Account.

Where to buy a refurbished Mac mini

U.S.: Amazon, Back Market, Best Buy, GainSaver, Mac of All Trades and Refurb.me.

U.K.: Affordable Mac, Amazon, Back Market, Hoxton Macs, MacFinder, Mac4Sale and MusicMagpie.

Two L-shaped blocks of exposed concrete enclose it, one of them twice the height of the other, climbing from seven to fifteen stories as the ridge falls away toward the gulf four kilometers below. Concrete pylons spaced every fifteen meters carry the blocks down to a slope they never quite touch, opening porticoes deep enough to walk through, and above them the facades resolve into loggias at the scale of a single room. Seen from the coastal road, none of that is legible; one can only see a gray line drawn across the hills.

items.title: [Fast Company] What is public interest technology and how does it help people in need? A policy expert explains
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Every year, millions of people who qualify for food assistance never get it. The money exists and they meet the eligibility rules, but they don’t know that the program exists, or if they qualify. For others, the application is too long and complicated.

Public interest technology can fill these gaps between what a policy promises and what a person experiences.

Public interest technology is a combination of technology, data, design, policy, social science, ethics and law brought together to improve people’s lives and serve the common good. Public interest technology has prevented children from being poisoned by lead paint, helped families stay in their homes instead of being evicted, and supported disaster recovery efforts after the Los Angeles fires.

The work is carried out by government agencies, nonprofit organizations, universities, community groups and experts like me who study how to use technology to help solve societal issues.

How a solution arises

Public interest technology starts with identifying the problem and asking two questions: What system is not working for the people it is supposed to serve? And how can it be improved?

The next step involves building a cross-disciplinary team to address the situation and scoping the problem. A caseworker, for example, knows things that no analyst can discover from data. A community member knows the reality on the ground. Data scientists, designers, engineers and policy experts, as well as the people affected, create the technology together.

Once there is an initial design for a solution, the team iteratively develops the system, validates that it functions as intended, evaluates whether its impact is equitable, and field-tests it to reveal errors and measure impact.

Impact is the bottom line. A pilot program that ends in an academic paper or a press release does not help people. Impact means the system works, the community trusts it and uses it, and people’s lives improve.

Who the technology helps

Chicago used to wait until a child’s blood test came back positive for lead before inspecting a home for lead sources. That sequence protects the next child who will live there, but not the current one. A data-driven system that we helped develop tracks housing stock, building permits and health information in order to flag high-risk housing units, allowing the health department to conduct preventive inspections before a child gets poisoned.

Allegheny County, Pennsylvania, has a limited budget to help the 10,000 to 15,000 people who receive eviction notices each year. A machine learning system now identifies the residents most likely to become homeless, so the county’s limited outreach efforts and scarce dollars reach the people who need help the most.

Johnson County, Kansas, linked its jail system, emergency medical service and mental health service so it could identify people cycling between crisis and incarceration. The system helps mental health workers identify and reach out to people at risk before the next arrest.

Some cities are expanding public interest technology in-house. New York just launched the Public Interest Technology Crew, which embeds technology specialists in agencies to solve problems for residents. The first crew, embedded in the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection, is building a portal for New Yorkers to report violations of click-to-cancel subscription laws.

Organizations such as the U.S. Digital Corps, Coding it Forward and Data Science for Social Good (which I co-founded) are creating partnerships between technology specialists and employees in governments and nonprofits. And universities are starting to weave public interest technology into curricula, largely driven by the Public Interest Technology University Network, a consortium of universities, cities and foundations.

What makes a technology a public interest technology is a set of choices: who helps build it, how its success is defined, and who is accountable when it gets things wrong. Made correctly, those choices mean the person who qualifies for food assistance isn’t left waiting for it.
